title: Invisible Drifters
text: Take a deep breath and look at the palm of your hand.

title: Invisible Drifters
text: Right now, on your skin, in the air filling your lungs, and across every ocean on Earth,
nxt: trillions of microscopic entities are drifting in complete silence. They do not eat. They do not sleep.

title: Breaking the Rules
text: To understand why this question keeps scientists awake at night, you first have to realize how strange viruses truly are.

title: Breaking the Rules
text: If you look at a simple bacterium through a microscope, you see a living creature.
nxt: It consumes nutrients, produces energy, expels waste, and divides into two.

title: Breaking the Rules
text: But a virus breaks every one of those rules. Outside of a living host cell, a virus is as inert as dust.
nxt: It has no metabolism. It generates no energy.

title: The Hijack
text: Once inside, the virus hijacks the cellular machinery of the host.
nxt: It commands the cell to stop its normal work and turn entirely toward printing copies of the viral code.

text: And if viruses are not fully alive today, how could they have originated billions of years ago?
nxt: Did they emerge before the first cellular life, floating in the primordial soup of early Earth?

title: Virus First

title: Shrinking Parasites
text: This paradox led other researchers to propose a different path: the reduction hypothesis, sometimes called the regressive theory.

title: Shrinking Parasites
text: Instead of starting simple and staying simple, what if viruses started as complex living cells that degenerated over time?
nxt: In nature, organisms that adopt a parasitic lifestyle often shed unnecessary biological systems.

title: Shrinking Parasites

title: Shrinking Parasites
text: Imagine a primitive single-celled organism, billions of years ago, that began living inside a larger cell.

title: Escaped Genes
text: What if the first virus was born from within life itself?
nxt: Deep inside every living cell, genetic material is constantly moving, copying, and rearranging.

text: Certain segments of DNA, known as mobile genetic elements or jumping genes,
nxt: can cut and paste themselves into different places in a genome. They are restless travelers inside our own cellular blueprints.

title: Escaped Genes
text: The escape hypothesis suggests that, eons ago, a rogue piece of genetic code slipped free of its host cell.

title: Escaped Genes

title: Escaped Genes

title: Escaped Genes

title: Viruses of the Sea
text: Beyond our own bodies, viruses act as invisible puppet masters of global ecology.

title: Viruses of the Sea
text: Every second, an enormous number of infections take place in the ocean, mostly targeting bacteria and microscopic plankton.

title: Viruses of the Sea
text: When these microbes burst open, they release carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus back into the water, feeding the base of the marine food web.

title: Viruses of the Sea
text: Scientists call this recycling the viral shunt.
nxt: Nutrients locked inside living microbes are released again, so other plankton can use them, and the cycle starts over.

title: Viruses of the Sea

title: Viruses of the Sea
text: By culling microbes and recycling nutrients, viruses help keep the chemistry of the ocean in motion.
nxt: Without them, the flow of nutrients through the sea would look very different.
